## Proof

**Claim:** Yes, an injective function $f:\mathbb{R}\to\mathbb{R}$ can have countably many discontinuities. We construct an explicit example.

**Construction.** Let $\{q_n\}_{n=1}^{\infty}$ be an enumeration of $\mathbb{Q}$. Define
$$g(x) = \sum_{n=1}^{\infty} 2^{-n}\,\mathbf{1}_{[q_n,\infty)}(x), \qquad f(x) = x + g(x).$$

Since $\sum 2^{-n} < \infty$, the series defining $g$ converges absolutely and uniformly, so $g$ is well-defined and non-decreasing (each summand is non-decreasing). Hence $f = x + g$ is strictly increasing: for $x < y$,
$$f(y) - f(x) = (y - x) + \underbrace{(g(y)-g(x))}_{\geq 0} \geq y - x > 0.$$
A strictly increasing function is injective. ✓

**Discontinuities at rationals.** Fix $q_k$. From the left,
$$g(q_k^-) = \sum_{q_n < q_k} 2^{-n}, \qquad g(q_k) = \sum_{q_n \leq q_k} 2^{-n} = g(q_k^-) + 2^{-k}.$$
So $g$ has a jump of size $2^{-k} > 0$ at $q_k$, and since $x \mapsto x$ is continuous, $f$ has a jump discontinuity at every $q_k$. Thus $f$ is discontinuous at every rational.

**Continuity at irrationals.** Let $x_0 \in \mathbb{R}\setminus\mathbb{Q}$ and $\varepsilon > 0$. Choose $N$ with $\sum_{n>N} 2^{-n} < \varepsilon$. The finitely many points $q_1,\dots,q_N$ are all $\neq x_0$ (they are rational, $x_0$ is not), so choose $\delta > 0$ with $(x_0-\delta,\,x_0+\delta)$ avoiding $\{q_1,\dots,q_N\}$. For $|x - x_0| < \delta$, the indicators $\mathbf{1}_{[q_n,\infty)}$ for $n \leq N$ take the same value at $x$ and $x_0$, so
$$|g(x) - g(x_0)| \leq \sum_{n>N} 2^{-n} < \varepsilon.$$
Thus $g$ is continuous at $x_0$, and so $f = x + g$ is continuous at every irrational.

**Conclusion.** The function $f$ is injective (strictly increasing) and its set of discontinuities is exactly $\mathbb{Q}$, which is countably infinite. Therefore an injective function $\mathbb{R}\to\mathbb{R}$ **can** have countably many discontinuities. $\blacksquare$

### PROOF COMPLETE
